modules.content:
## A Moment of Real‑World Consequence Imagine you’ve just finished a vibrant, swirling pour on a 12‑inch canvas. The glossy surface looks perfect—until you notice a faint, tingling sensation on the back of your hand. You glance down and see a thin film of uncured resin that you inadvertently brushed off while cleaning your tools. Within minutes the skin feels tight, slightly red, and a faint metallic smell lingers in the air. What just happened? You’ve been exposed to the same chemicals that can cause skin irritation, respiratory discomfort, and long‑term sensitisation if proper protection isn’t used. This scenario is far more common than you might think; a quick survey of beginner resin artists on online forums shows that **over 40 %** experienced at least one mild skin reaction in their first month of pouring. The good news? With a few simple, inexpensive safeguards, you can eliminate those risks and keep your creative flow uninterrupted. The following sections walk you through everything you need to know to protect yourself from fumes and skin contact while working with epoxy resin. --- ## 1. Why Epoxy Resin Needs Respect ### 1.1 What Is Epoxy Resin? Epoxy resin is a two‑part polymer system consisting of: | Component | Common Name | Role | |-----------|-------------|------| | **Part A** | Resin (or base) | Provides the bulk of the polymer matrix | | **Part B** | Hardener (or catalyst) | Triggers the chemical reaction that turns the liquid mixture into a solid, durable plastic | When the two parts are mixed in the correct ratio (usually 1 : 1 by volume or weight), a **cross‑linking reaction** occurs, forming a hard, glass‑like surface. This reaction releases **volatile organic compounds (VOCs)**—tiny molecules that evaporate into the air—and can also generate heat. ### 1.2 Chemical Hazards at a Glance | Hazard | How It Affects You | Typical Exposure Sources | |--------|-------------------|--------------------------| | **Skin irritation / sensitisation** | Redness, itching, rash; repeated exposure can lead to allergic reactions | Direct contact with uncured resin or hardener | | **Respiratory irritation** | Coughing, throat tightness, shortness of breath | Inhalation of VOCs and fine resin droplets | | **Eye irritation** | Stinging, tearing, blurred vision | Splashing of uncured mixture into the eyes | | **Heat generation** | Burns if large volumes cure in a confined space | Exothermic (heat‑producing) reaction during curing | Even though cured epoxy is inert and safe to handle, the **uncured mixture** is where the danger lies. The key to safety is treating every batch as hazardous until it is fully cured. --- ## 2. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Essentials ### 2.1 Core PPE Items | PPE | Why It’s Needed | How to Choose | |-----|----------------|---------------| | **Gloves** | Prevent direct skin contact with resin and hardener | • **Nitrile** (preferred) – resistant to chemicals, puncture‑proof, comfortable for fine work.
• **Latex** – cheaper but can degrade faster and may cause allergic reactions.
• **Vinyl** – acceptable for light tasks but less durable. | | **Respirator** | Filters inhaled VOCs and fine droplets | • **N95 or higher respirator** – captures particles but not gases; only suitable if VOC levels are low.
• **Half‑mask respirator with organic vapor cartridges** – the best choice for most indoor resin work.
• **Full‑face respirator** – provides eye protection plus breathing filtration; ideal for large projects or poor ventilation. | | **Safety goggles** (or face shield) | Shields eyes from splashes and airborne particles | • **Wrap‑around goggles** – seal around the eyes, preventing vapor ingress.
• **Face shield** – used in conjunction with goggles for maximum coverage during mixing. | | **Protective clothing** | Stops resin from soaking into everyday clothes | • **Reusable lab coat** or **disposable coveralls** made of polyester/cotton blend.
• **Long sleeves** and **pants** – avoid exposing skin. | | **Footwear** | Prevents accidental spills from reaching the floor | • Closed‑toe shoes; consider **chemical‑resistant boots** for larger studios. | > **Tip:** Keep a spare set of gloves nearby. If you notice tears, punctures, or a loss of elasticity, replace them immediately—don’t gamble with compromised protection. ### 2.2 How to Don and Doff PPE Correctly 1. **Preparation** – Wash hands with mild soap; dry thoroughly. 2. **Gloves** – Pull them on, ensuring the cuffs extend past the wrist. Scrunch the fingers to eliminate gaps. 3. **Goggles** – Place them over the eyes, adjust the strap for a snug but comfortable fit. 4. **Respirator** – a. Hold the mask to the face, place the straps over the head.
b. Pull the lower strap over the nose and mouth, then the upper strap over the crown.
c. Perform a **user seal check** (inhale sharply; the mask should collapse slightly, and you shouldn’t feel air leaking). 5. **Protective clothing** – Slip into the lab coat or coveralls, button or zip up fully. When the session ends, **remove PPE in reverse order** to avoid contaminating your skin or clothing: 1. Gloves → 2. Respirator → 3. Goggles → 4. Coveralls. Dispose of single‑use items in a sealed bag and wash reusable PPE according to the manufacturer’s instructions. --- ## 3. Building a Well‑Ventilated Workspace ### 3.1 Why Ventilation Matters Ventilation dilutes airborne VOCs, lowering their concentration to a level that is unlikely to cause irritation. The **American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH)** recommends an **exposure limit** for many organic vapors of **0.5 ppm** (parts per million) averaged over an 8‑hour workday. While exact limits for epoxy resin vary, keeping the air exchange rate high is a practical, low‑cost safety measure. ### 3.2 Designing the Ideal Pour Area 1. **Location** – Choose a room with at least one operable window and a door that can stay open. 2. **Airflow Direction** – Set up **cross‑ventilation**: air should flow **into** the room from one side (window) and **out** from the opposite side (door or second window). 3. **Fans** – * **Box fan** or **oscillating fan** placed near the inlet draws fresh air in. * **Exhaust fan** (or a second box fan) positioned near the outlet pushes contaminated air out. * For small studios, a **window exhaust fan** (often used for dryer venting) can be very effective. 4. **Air Quality Monitor (optional)** – A low‑cost VOC sensor can give real‑time feedback, helping you decide when to increase airflow. ### 3.3 Practical Ventilation Checklist - [ ] Open a window at least 6 inches wide. - [ ] Position a fan to blow air **into** the workspace. - [ ] Place a second fan or open a door to let air **escape**. - [ ] Keep the fan(s) running for **15 minutes before** mixing and **throughout** the curing period (typically 24 h for standard epoxy). - [ ] If you notice a strong chemical smell, increase fan speed or add an additional fan. > **Quick Test:** Hold your hand a few inches above the resin surface while the fans run. If you feel a faint breeze and the odor is faint, ventilation is likely adequate. --- ## 4. Safe Handling Practices ### 4.1 Preparing the Mix 1. **Measure Precisely** – Use separate, clean measuring cups for resin and hardener. Follow the manufacturer’s ratio exactly; an off‑balance mix can increase VOC release and cause incomplete curing. 2. **Mix Slowly** – Stir gently for **3–5 minutes** to minimise bubbles. Rapid mixing can trap air, leading to more vapour release during curing. 3. **Use a Dedicated Mixing Surface** – A silicone mat or disposable plastic sheet prevents resin from soaking into the workbench. ### 4.2 Pouring and Working - **Avoid Direct Spraying** – Instead of shaking the mixed resin, pour it slowly from a height of 6–12 inches to reduce aerosol formation. - **Keep Tools Wet** – Dipping brushes or stir sticks in a small tray of resin prevents them from drying and sticking, reducing the chance of accidental splashes. ### 4.3 Cleaning Up | Cleaning Tool | Use For | How | |---------------|---------|-----| | **Isopropyl alcohol (≥ 70 %)** | Small spills, tool cleaning | Dampen a paper towel, wipe the area; dispose of the saturated towel in a sealed bag. | | **Soap and warm water** | Resin that has cured | Scrub gently; cured epoxy is inert and can be removed with standard detergents. | | **Dedicated waste container** | Uncured resin leftovers | Seal the container tightly and label it “hazardous waste – epoxy resin.” Follow local disposal regulations. | Never rinse uncured resin down the sink; it can harden in pipes and cause blockages. ### 4.4 Emergency Procedures - **Skin Contact:** 1. Remove contaminated clothing immediately. 2. Rinse the affected area with **copious amounts of water** for at least **15 minutes**. 3. Wash with mild soap. 4. Seek medical attention if irritation persists. - **Eye Exposure:** 1. Flush eyes with clean water or saline for **15 minutes** while holding the eyelids open. 2. Do not rub the eyes. 3. Obtain medical care promptly. - **Inhalation:** 1. Move to fresh air immediately. 2. If breathing is difficult, seek professional medical help. - **Spill Management:** 1. Contain the spill with absorbent pads or sand. 2. Scoop the solidified resin into a waste container. 3. Dispose of according to local hazardous‑waste guidelines. --- ## 5. Maintaining Your Protective Gear | Item | Maintenance Routine | Replacement Frequency | |------|---------------------|------------------------| | **Nitrile gloves** | Inspect for tears before each use; wash hands after removal. | Every **30 minutes** of continuous work or sooner if damaged. | | **Respirator cartridges** | Store in a sealed container away from heat; label with date of first use. | Replace after **8 hours** of exposure or per manufacturer’s “service life” rating. | | **Goggles** | Rinse with warm water, wipe with lint‑free cloth. | Replace if scratches or fogging impair visibility. | | **Lab coat** | Machine‑wash on a gentle cycle; air‑dry. | Replace when resin stains become permanent or fabric thins. | Regular inspection not only prolongs the life of your PPE but also ensures that you remain protected throughout each session. --- ## 6. A Simple Safety Checklist – Before You Begin | ✅ | Action | |----|--------| | 1 | Verify that the workspace is well‑ventilated (windows open, fans positioned). | | 2 | Don all required PPE (nitrile gloves, respirator with proper cartridge, goggles, lab coat). | | 3 | Check that measuring cups and mixing tools are clean and dry. | | 4 | Review the resin‑to‑hardener ratio on the product label. | | 5 | Prepare a waste container for leftover uncured resin. | | 6 | Keep a first‑aid kit, eye‑wash station, and fire extinguisher (Class B) nearby. | | 7 | Perform a brief “smell test” – if the odor feels strong, increase ventilation before mixing. | | 8 | After mixing, stir slowly for the recommended time; avoid splashing. | | 9 | Pour from a modest height to minimise aerosol generation. | |10 | After the pour, clean tools with isopropyl alcohol while wearing gloves. | |11 | Dispose of waste according to local regulations. | |12 | Remove PPE in the proper order and wash hands thoroughly. | Having this checklist printed and posted in your studio reinforces habit formation and reduces the chance of oversight. --- ## ## Key Takeaways - **Epoxy resin’s uncured state is chemically active** and can irritate skin, eyes, and lungs; once cured, it is inert and safe. - **Core PPE** for resin pouring includes nitrile gloves, a respirator with organic‑vapor cartridges (or at least an N95 in low‑VOC settings), safety goggles, and protective clothing. - **Ventilation is non‑negotiable**: cross‑flow of fresh air, aided by fans, keeps VOC levels low and protects your respiratory health. - **Safe handling**—accurate measuring, slow mixing, careful pouring, and proper clean‑up—minimises exposure to hazardous fumes and splashes. - **Immediate response** to skin, eye, or inhalation incidents (rinse, move to fresh air, seek medical help) prevents escalation. - **Regular maintenance and replacement** of PPE ensure continued protection; a simple checklist can embed safety into every pour. By integrating these practices into every resin‑art session, you safeguard your health while letting your creativity flow unhindered. Happy pouring!

modules.title: Understanding Epoxy Resin Components
modules.content:
## What Happens When You Open a New Bottle of Resin?

Imagine you have just bought a 500 ml bottle of clear epoxy resin for your first “pour‑painting” project. You pour the contents into a clean cup, add a splash of metallic pigment, and stir. Within minutes the mixture turns cloudy, a faint heat rises from the cup, and a sticky film forms on the rim. You’ve just witnessed the chemistry of epoxy in action—and also a common mistake: the resin and hardener were not mixed in the exact proportion required for that batch.

Understanding **why** the correct ratio matters, what each component does, and how long the mixture stays workable is the foundation of successful resin art. This chapter walks you through the chemistry, the math, and the practical steps you need to master before you even touch a brush.

---

## 1. The Two‑Part System: Part A and Part B

Epoxy resin is a **two‑component thermosetting polymer**. The two bottles you see on the shelf are not “resin” and “hardener” in the vague sense; they are **Part A (the resin)** and **Part B (the hardener)**.  

* **Part A – The Base Resin**  
  * Contains epoxy oligomers (the “building blocks”) and a low‑viscosity solvent that makes the mixture fluid.  
  * Provides the **clear, glossy matrix** that will encapsulate pigments, objects, and any additive you introduce.  

* **Part B – The Hardener (Curing Agent)**  
  * Holds a **cross‑linking agent**—typically an amine or anhydride—that reacts with the epoxy groups in Part A.  
  * Initiates the **cross‑linking reaction** that turns the liquid into a solid polymer network.  

When the two parts combine, they undergo a **cross‑linking reaction** that transforms the mixture from a fluid state to a rigid, glass‑like solid. This reaction is **exothermic** (it releases heat) and proceeds until all reactive groups are exhausted, at which point the material is said to be **cured**.

> **Why the ratio matters:** The stoichiometry (the exact proportion of reactive groups) is fixed. Too much resin leaves unreacted hardener, which can cause a sticky surface and potential **skin irritation / sensitisation**. Too much hardener leaves unreacted resin, leading to a tacky finish and possible **respiratory irritation** from off‑gassing.

---

## 2. Mixing Ratios: From Theory to the Kitchen Counter

### 2.1 Standard Ratios

Most commercial epoxy systems are formulated to cure at a **1 : 1 weight ratio** (i.e., 100 g of Part A to 100 g of Part B). Some specialty resins use **2 : 1** or **4 : 1** ratios, but the label will always specify the required proportion. The ratio is expressed as:

```
(resin weight) : (hardener weight) = X : Y
```

> **Note:** The ratio is based on **weight**, not volume. Because the densities of Part A and Part B can differ, a volume‑based measurement must be calibrated with the manufacturer’s “mixing cup” instructions.

### 2.2 Converting Between Weight and Volume

If you prefer to measure by volume (using the provided mixing cup), follow these steps:

1. **Locate the density values** on the product data sheet (e.g., 1.12 g/ml for resin, 1.08 g/ml for hardener).  
2. **Calculate the weight** of the volume you intend to use:  
   \[
   \text{Weight}_\text{Resin} = \text{Volume}_\text{Resin} \times \text{Density}_\text{Resin}
   \]  
   \[
   \text{Weight}_\text{Hardener} = \text{Volume}_\text{Hardener} \times \text{Density}_\text{Hardener}
   \]  
3. **Adjust the volumes** until the weight ratio matches the required X : Y.  

A quick example: For a 1 : 1 weight ratio, if you pour **30 ml of resin** (30 ml × 1.12 g/ml = 33.6 g), you need **31 ml of hardener** (31 ml × 1.08 g/ml ≈ 33.5 g). The manufacturer’s mixing cup often includes a **marked line** that already accounts for these density differences, so you can simply fill to the line for each component.

### 2.3 Using a Scale

Because weight is the most reliable metric, many seasoned artists use a digital kitchen scale:

1. **Tare** the scale with an empty mixing cup.  
2. **Add Part A** until the desired weight is reached (e.g., 100 g).  
3. **Reset the scale** (tare again) and **add Part B** to the same weight.  

**Advantages of weighing:**  
* Eliminates errors caused by temperature‑related volume changes.  
* Works with any brand, regardless of cup design.  

**When to weigh:**  
* When mixing large batches (≥ 250 ml).  
* When working with low‑viscosity “fast‑cure” resins where even a 1 % deviation can cause defects.

---

## 3. Additives: Extending the Palette Without Breaking the Chemistry

Once you have a correctly mixed base, you can enrich it with a variety of **additives**. Each additive must be compatible with the epoxy system; otherwise, it can interfere with the cross‑linking reaction or cause premature curing.

| Additive Type | Typical Use | Compatibility Tips |
|---------------|-------------|--------------------|
| **Pigments (powders, inks, mica)** | Color, opacity, sparkle | Use **oil‑based** or **epoxy‑compatible** pigments; avoid water‑based inks unless they are specifically labeled “resin‑safe.” |
| **Dyes (alcohol‑based)** | Transparent hues | Add **slowly** (1 % wt of total mix) to avoid over‑dilution, which reduces cross‑link density. |
| **UV Inhibitors (e.g., Tinuvin 327)** | Prevent yellowing from sunlight | Typically added at **0.1 % wt**; ensure the inhibitor is soluble in the resin phase. |
| **Thickeners (fumed silica, silicone‑based)** | Create “high‑flow” or “gel” textures for 3‑D pours | Add **after** the resin and hardener are fully blended; over‑thickening can trap air and lengthen pot life. |
| **Flexibilizers (polyurethane additives)** | Increase impact resistance | Use only if the manufacturer lists a compatible flexibilizer; otherwise, you risk **incomplete curing**. |

> **Key rule:** **Never add pigments or additives before the resin and hardener are fully combined.** Adding them too early can create pockets where the hardener cannot reach the resin, leading to soft spots and surface tackiness.

---

## 4. Measuring Accurately: Tools and Techniques

### 4.1 The Mixing Cup – Your First Line of Defense

The **mixing cup** supplied with most epoxy kits is calibrated for the recommended ratio. To use it correctly:

1. **Place the cup on a flat, level surface** (avoid wobbling that can cause uneven volumes).  
2. **Pour Part A** until the **inner rim** of the cup is reached. Do **not** fill past the line; surface tension can create a false “full” appearance.  
3. **Repeat for Part B** using the same cup.  

**Common mistake:** Using the same cup for both components without cleaning the rim first. A thin film of resin on the rim can cause the hardener volume to be slightly less, throwing off the ratio.

### 4.2 Graduated Syringes – For Small Batches

When mixing less than 100 ml, a **graduated syringe** (10 ml, 20 ml, or 30 ml) offers high precision:

* **Draw Part A** to the exact mark.  
* **Flush the syringe** with a small amount of solvent (e.g., isopropyl alcohol) to clear residue, then **draw Part B** to the same mark.  

**Tip:** Keep the syringe upright while drawing to avoid air bubbles that can distort the measured volume.

### 4.3 Digital Scales – Best for Consistency

A **digital kitchen scale** with at least 0.1 g resolution is ideal for repeatable results. When using a scale:

* **Zero** the scale with the empty mixing container.  
* **Add resin** first, then **tare** again before adding hardener.  

**Pitfall to avoid:** Placing the scale on a **vibrating surface** (e.g., near a running fan) can cause fluctuating readings. Use a stable, flat countertop.

---

## 5. Pot Life and Working Time: The Clock Starts When You Mix

### 5.1 Definitions

* **Pot Life** – The period after mixing during which the resin remains fluid enough to work with. It ends when the mixture becomes too viscous to stir or pour.  
* **Working Time** – A subset of pot life; the interval you have to **apply** the mixture (e.g., pour, spread, embed objects) before it begins to set.

Both are temperature‑dependent: higher ambient temperatures **shorten** pot life, while cooler environments **extend** it.

### 5.2 Typical Values

| Ambient Temp (°C) | Approx. Pot Life (min) |
|-------------------|------------------------|
| 20 °C (68 °F) | 30–45 |
| 25 °C (77 °F) | 20–30 |
| 30 °C (86 °F) | 15–20 |

> **Remember:** The numbers above are **guidelines**. The exact values depend on the specific resin formulation and the presence of additives (e.g., thickeners will reduce pot life).

### 5.3 Managing Pot Life

1. **Pre‑cool your tools** (mixing cup, stir stick) if you expect a fast‑cure resin. A few minutes in the refrigerator can add valuable seconds.  
2. **Work in a temperature‑controlled space** (ideally 20–22 °C). If you must work in a warmer workshop, consider **using a fan** to disperse heat generated by the exothermic reaction.  
3. **Mix in smaller batches**. If a project requires 300 ml of resin, mix **three 100 ml batches** sequentially rather than one large batch; each smaller batch retains a longer working window.  

### 5.4 Recognizing the End of Working Time

* **Viscosity increase** – The mixture feels thicker on the stir stick; it no longer flows freely.  
* **Heat buildup** – A noticeable rise in temperature (you can feel it with the back of your hand) signals that the cross‑linking reaction is accelerating.  
* **Surface changes** – Small bubbles start to **pop** or a thin film forms on the tops of the mixture.

When any of these signs appear, **stop adding pigments or objects** and proceed to the next step (e.g., pouring or curing) before the mixture becomes unmanageable.

---

## 6. Practical Workflow: From Empty Bottle to Ready‑to‑Pour

Below is a **step‑by‑step checklist** that integrates accurate measuring, additive handling, and pot‑life management. Follow it each time you start a pour:

1. **Gather PPE** (gloves, respirator, goggles) as covered in the **Safety** chapter.  
2. **Set up a clean, level mixing station**; place a **digital scale** and mixing cup within easy reach.  
3. **Determine batch size** (e.g., 200 ml total). Calculate the required resin and hardener weights (e.g., 100 g each for a 1 : 1 system).  
4. **Weigh Part A** into the cup, then **weigh Part B** to match the target weight.  
5. **Stir gently** for **30–45 seconds** using a **silicone‑spatula**. Scrape the sides and bottom to ensure a uniform blend.  
6. **Add pigments/additives** **after** the base is fully mixed. Add in **small increments**, stirring **10 seconds** between each addition.  
7. **Check viscosity**: lift the stir stick; the mixture should flow off the tip in a slow, steady stream.  
8. **Start your pour** within the **working time window** (usually the first 5–10 minutes).  
9. **Cover the workpiece** with a dust‑free lid or box to protect the curing surface.  

**If pot life ends before you finish pouring:**  
* **Stop adding more mixture** and let the current batch cure.  
* **Prepare a fresh batch** for any remaining areas, remembering that a partially cured layer can bond to a fresh layer if the surface is still tacky.  

---

## 7. Troubleshooting Common Mixing Errors

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Remedy |
|---------|--------------|--------|
| **Sticky surface after cure** | Hardener under‑ratio (too much resin) or insufficient mixing | Re‑measure using a scale; mix at least 60 seconds longer. |
| **Cloudy or milky appearance** | Over‑ratio of hardener, or contamination with moisture | Verify ratio; ensure mixing tools are dry; discard the batch if contaminated. |
| **Excessive heat (burning smell)** | Large volume in a confined space; fast‑cure resin; high ambient temperature | Reduce batch size; improve ventilation; use a heat‑resistant silicone mat. |
| **Bubbles that won’t rise** | High viscosity from thickeners or low temperature | Warm the mixture gently (30 °C water bath) and stir gently to release trapped air. |
| **Surface skin formation (skin on top of the mix)** | Working time exceeded; mixture left idle too long | Use a **heat gun** or **torch** briefly to break the skin, then stir gently. |

---

## 8. Frequently Asked Questions

**Q1. Can I use a kitchen measuring cup instead of the supplied mixing cup?**  
*Only if you convert the volumes using the resin and hardener densities.* A kitchen cup lacks the calibration needed for the exact ratio, so it is prone to error.

**Q2. Is it okay to add more hardener to speed up curing?**  
*No.* Adding extra hardener disrupts the stoichiometric balance, leading to a brittle finish and possible **skin irritation** from excess amine.

**Q3. How do I know if an additive is “compatible”?**  
Look for the term **“epoxy‑compatible”** on the product label, or consult the resin manufacturer’s data sheet. If uncertain, test a **small 10 ml batch** first.

**Q4. Does the pot life change if I add pigments?**  
Yes. Pigments can **increase viscosity**, slightly shortening working time. Adjust your workflow accordingly.

**Q5. Can I store mixed resin for later use?**  
Mixed epoxy will **self‑cure**; it cannot be re‑used once the reaction has begun. Dispose of any leftover mixture according to local hazardous waste regulations.

---

## 9. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

- **Ratio:** Follow the **weight‑based** ratio printed on the label (commonly 1 : 1).  
- **Measuring tools:** Digital scale > graduated syringe > manufacturer’s mixing cup.  
- **Additive rule:** Add **after** full resin‑hardener blend; keep additive concentration ≤ 5 % wt unless otherwise specified.  
- **Pot life:** 30–45 min at 20 °C; decreases ~10 % per 5 °C rise.  
- **Working time:** Aim to finish pouring within **10 minutes** of mixing for most standard resins.  

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Part A (resin) and Part B (hardener) must be combined in the exact weight ratio** specified by the manufacturer; volume measurements are only reliable when the cup is calibrated for that specific formulation.  
- **Accurate measuring**—preferably with a digital scale—prevents under‑ or over‑curing, which causes sticky, cloudy, or brittle finishes.  
- **Additives** (pigments, dyes, UV inhibitors, thickeners) can be safely used **only after** the resin and hardener are fully mixed, and only if they are labeled epoxy‑compatible.  
- **Pot life and working time** are temperature‑dependent; keep ambient conditions stable, work in manageable batch sizes, and monitor viscosity and heat to avoid premature curing.  
- A **systematic workflow**—measure, mix, add, stir, pour—combined with proper PPE ensures consistent, high‑quality resin art while minimizing health risks.
